name: Granum / LMN
tagline: Vertical software for landscape and lawn care contractors: customer records, estimates priced off labor and material rates, and job costing back against the budget.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The part most crews actually touch, a customer list plus an estimate that multiplies production rates by crew hours and spits out a proposal, is a weekend build and honestly closer to a spreadsheet than a platform. An agent can give you a local app with a cost catalog, templated services, markup rules, and a printable proposal, and it will be faster than the real thing because it only has your workflow in it. What does not come along is everything downstream of the estimate: crew clock-in on phones, payroll-grade time data, accounting sync, and the budgeting model that tells you what your overhead recovery per hour should actually be. Those industry cost defaults and the training material around them are a real part of what you are buying, not just packaging. Build it if you already know your numbers; keep paying if the software is the reason you know them.
coreLoopDIY: A local web app where you keep customers, build estimates from a saved catalog of labor and material rates with markup and overhead recovery baked in, and print a clean proposal PDF.
requirements: Node 20 and a machine you can run it on
Your own labor rates, material costs and overhead numbers to seed the catalog
whatYouLose: Crew mobile app: clock-in, geofencing, timesheets that feed payroll
QuickBooks or Xero sync, so job costing stops at your own manual entry
Industry cost and production rate defaults you can sanity-check yours against
The budgeting and overhead-recovery training that makes the pricing model make sense
Someone to call when a bid goes out wrong in April
moatNotes: The estimating math is arithmetic. The defensible parts are payroll and accounting plumbing plus a decade of contractor cost benchmarks and the education layer that teaches the pricing model.
whyPeopleStillPay: Most of the money in this category is not the quoting screen, it is the fact that hours punched by a crew at 6am end up in payroll and back against the job budget without anyone retyping them. A self-built estimator gives you a nice proposal and a spreadsheet that goes stale the moment work starts. Contractors also pay for the pricing framework itself: recover overhead per production hour, price by crew hour, know your break-even. If you already run that model in your head, the software is a convenience. If you learned it from the software, cancelling costs more than the subscription.
notes: Fine one-shot if you only live in the quoting screen, which is a surprising number of people.
prompt:
Build a local-first estimating and job tracking app for a small landscaping contractor. No accounts, no cloud, no telemetry, single user on their own machine.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Next.js 14 App Router with TypeScript
- SQLite via better-sqlite3, file at ./data/app.db, schema created on boot if missing
- Tailwind CSS, plain server actions, no external UI kit
- Proposal PDFs via a print-optimised route and browser print-to-PDF, no headless Chrome dependency

Data model:
- customers: name, contact, address, notes
- catalog_items: name, kind (labor | material | equipment | subcontract), unit, unit_cost, default_production_rate (units per crew hour, nullable)
- service_templates: named bundles of catalog items with quantities, so mow, mulch install, spring cleanup are one click
- estimates: customer, status (draft | sent | won | lost), overhead_recovery_per_hour, target_margin_pct, line items with qty, unit_cost snapshot, and computed price
- jobs: created from a won estimate, copies the budgeted hours and material costs
- time_entries and cost_entries: manual entry against a job, date, hours or amount, note

Behaviour:
- Estimate pricing: labor lines derive crew hours from quantity divided by production rate, cost equals hours times unit_cost, then add overhead_recovery_per_hour times hours, then apply target margin to reach price. Show cost, overhead, margin and price side by side and let the user override any line price.
- Job view: budgeted hours and cost versus actual from entries, with variance in dollars and percent, red when over.
- Settings page for default overhead recovery rate and margin, plus company name and address used on proposals.
- Proposal view: clean single page, line descriptions with prices only (never expose cost or margin), optional terms text block, print stylesheet that fits A4 and US Letter.
- Seed script with a handful of example catalog items and one template, clearly marked as placeholder numbers to replace.
- CSV export for customers, estimates and time entries.

Explicitly out of scope, do not attempt: mobile crew app, GPS or geofencing, payroll, accounting sync, e-signature, email sending, multi-user auth, route optimisation.

Any secrets go in .env with a committed .env.example. Ship a README with setup, the pricing formula written out in plain English, and a short note that the seeded rates are fake.
